summary: A 1970 note with protocol notes for the ARPA Network. It collects the author's thoughts on ideas being discussed for the network's protocols. It is a discussion paper, not a standard.

eli5.summary: The author wrote down their thoughts on how the network's rules should work, like a student's notes during a class discussion.

questions: what is an ncp network control program
subtitle: Proposal for a simple, extensible host-to-host protocol with socket-based communication

tldr.problem: The ARPA Network needs a protocol that all participants can implement and agree on. Earlier proposals were too complex; something simpler but still extensible is needed.
tldr.mechanism: Meyer proposes a three-level hierarchy: the IMP network (hardware), the Network Control Program (NCP) at each host (software), and a User Control and Communication protocol (UCC) for login. NCPs communicate via sockets (unique identifiers for send and receive points) and manage connections through commands like RFC, CLS, and INT.
tldr.outcome: This proposal became the foundation for the ARPANET's first host protocol, establishing concepts like socket-based communication that persist in modern networking.

facts.label: Socket code size
facts.value: 8 bits (128 send + 128 receive sockets per process)

today: RFC 46 is not a standard, but it established the foundational concepts for the first ARPANET host protocol. The socket model, NCP, and layered approach shaped the design of TCP/IP and persist in modern networking APIs and architectures.

sections.title: Three-Level Protocol Hierarchy
sections.content: Meyer proposes viewing the network as three layers of increasing generality. The bottom layer is the IMP network, which moves raw messages between host computers. Above it is the Network Control Program (NCP), a privileged module in each host that factors the IMP's capabilities into communication paths between programs. At the top is the User Control and Communication (UCC) protocol, which handles user login and process creation at remote hosts. This layered view allows each layer to evolve independently while keeping network communication simple.
sections.eli5: Imagine three floors: the bottom floor has the mailroom (the IMP), the middle floor has the switchboard operator (the NCP), and the top floor has the secretary who helps you log in (the UCC).

sections.title: Socket Connections and NCP Commands
sections.content: Communication happens through sockets, unique 48-bit identifiers that identify which program is sending and which is receiving. Each socket has a state: inactive, open, or connected. The NCP manages connections by exchanging control commands over a reserved link: RFC to request connection, CLS to close it, INT to interrupt a process, BLK to block output when buffers fill, and RSM to resume. An event queue at each socket holds pending connection requests and notifications, allowing programs to manage asynchronous activity without blocking.
sections.eli5: Each program gets a numbered mailbox (a socket). Programs send commands like "request connection" or "close connection" through a special control line, and each mailbox keeps a queue of events that happened to it.

sections.title: Application Interface
sections.content: Meyer outlines a set of function calls applications use: LISTEN to open a receive socket and watch for requests, INIT to request connection to a foreign socket, STATUS to check for events, ACCEPT or REJECT to handle requests, CLOSE to disconnect, and TRANSMIT to send or receive data. The RFC includes an example where process A initiates connection with process B, showing how the loggers then drop out and the two processes communicate directly over the established link. This simple interface hides the complexity of socket management from applications.
sections.eli5: Programs call LISTEN to wait for calls, INIT to call someone else, ACCEPT or REJECT to answer, and TRANSMIT to send or receive messages, just like a telephone.

sections.title: Design Rationale
sections.content: Meyer emphasizes simplicity and extensibility. The protocol is simple enough for all sites to implement and agree on, without over-specifying implementation details. The layers allow higher-level complexity (like the UCC protocol for login) to be added above without changing the core NCP. The RFC explicitly reserves dynamic reconnection for future implementation, rejecting attempts to solve every problem at once. This focused approach proved successful: the basic concepts of sockets and simplex connections became central to the Internet.
sections.eli5: The idea is to keep the rules simple so everyone can build it, but leave room to add more features later. Don't try to solve every problem on the first try.
